newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait Central Bank asks banks to set loan limit.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait Central Bank asks banks to set loan limit.

text.p: Kuwait's Central Bank has asked local banks to cap lending for equity trading at current levels in an effort to stabilise the bourse, economists said on Sunday.

They said that Governor Sheikh Salem Abdul-Aziz al-Sabah held a low-profile meeting earlier this month with Kuwait's top bankers to discuss measures aimed at averting a financial crisis after the Kuwait Stock Exchange set record highs.
"The Central Bank later sent banks a memo asking them to maintain lending for equity trading at current levels to contain demand on the bourse," said economist Jassem al-Saadoun.

The index, which rose by about 40 percent a year for the past two years, closed 5.1 points lower on Sunday at 2,339.9. On April 27 it peaked at a record 2,354.7, triggering heated debates in parliament and warnings of a possible crash.

Bankers and economists said at the time the market was expected to correct after a period of over-heating in which the prices of some shares soared mainly due to heavy speculation by key investors not based on fundamentals.
Kuwait has six commercial banks, two specialised banks and an Islamic financial institution.

Bankers could not provide an exact figure for loans extended for equity trading but they estimate that between 300 million and 400 million dinars ($993.4 million to $1.33 billion) were provided to stock exchange investors by the local banks.
"The Governor spoke of limits on margin loans, overdrafts and personal loans which are all directly involved in trading," said Saadoun. "There are also indirect loans which are involved in trading."

In late April, trading value on the exchange soared to 125.8 million dinars during a single 2-1/2 hour session in which 445 million shares were traded. In the week to last Wednesday the daily traded average fell to a modest 37 million dinars while volume eased to an average 119.4 million shares.

In 1982 Kuwait's unregulated Souq Manakh bourse crashed, resulting in a debt of over $20 billion which the government is still trying to resolve. The state at the time stepped in to buy shares in many companies, which it is now selling in a privatisation programme.

Economists in oil-rich Kuwait have urged the government to clearly tell investors that it would not bail them out again in cases of heavy losses although they say the exchange has several measures in place to avoid a repetition of 1982. ($=0.30 dinar)
